the distinct mechanisms of ionic modulation underlie GABA actions in the pyramdal cell and interneuron groups during the induction of seizure‐like activity.

the GABA‐dependent afterdischarges induced in the hippocampus in vitro were initiated by a biphasic Cl‐intrusion in pyramidal neurons, which was enhanced by the glutamatergically driven slow depolarization.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying the generation of epileptiform activity, which may be a useful model of human epileptic seizures.

the ionic mechanisms of GABAergic transmission in pyramidal neurons and interneurons in the rat hippocampi, and with the ionic modulation of seizure‐like after discharges.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GABAergic responses of the pyramidal neurons were more sensitive to ionic modulation than those of the interneurons.

the seizure‐like network activities are initiated by the GABA‐dependent depolarizing shift in the reversal potential of GABAergic responses, which are driven by the GABAergic input and enhanced by glutamergic neuron excitation.
GABA conversion is induced in the pyramical cell group, and the GABA reversal potentials are elevated above spike threshold in the pyramdial cells, but not in the interneurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a seizure‐like network state is induced in the CA1 area in response to electrical stimuli by the transient conversion of GABA‐mediated hyperpolarization to depolarization and/or excitatory postsynaptic potentials in pyramidal neurons, and that the conversion is induced by the accumulation of extracellular Cl– and K+ in the CA1 network, which is mediated by the GABA‐ and the glutamate‐dependent slow depolariation, respectively.

the GABAergic network activity is modulated by ionic mechanisms in a cell type‐specific manner and the ionic mechanisms underlying the slow depolarizing GABA response are distinct from those underlying the GABA‐dependent epileptiform afterdischarge.

the seizure‐like activity in the hippocampal CA3–CA1 area is initiated by the slow depolarizing GABAergic response that is enhanced by the glutamatergics, and that this slow GABA response is composed of two distinct phases of GABAA‐dependent Cl– accumulation and K+‐dependent Cl– influx, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GABAergic signals can be rapidly and transiently converted from inhibitory to excitatory, and that this conversion may be the critical step in the initiation of epileptiform activity.

the GABAergic slow depolarization that is a hallmark of seizure‐like activity in the normal hippocampal CA3 area is a result of the activation of GABAA receptors and glutamatergric ionotropic receptors.
we have identified a mechanism by which the GABA reversal potentials in pyramidal neurons are elevated to spike threshold levels during the slow depolrization.
